findings.summary: A request whose record ended `bound` (or whose summary never arrived) with no recorded call and no thrown fetch now reports `costUsd: 0`, which reads as known free. The image door treats a cut-short run as unknown.
findings.failureScenario: A speech request is cut off by the 1-hour RECORD_MAX_MS bound, or its handler hangs while an upstream call is in flight. The sink has `lost == 0` and `calls == 0`, so `sink.lost <= sink.calls.length` holds. The `request` step then records `costUsd: 0`, with `complete: false` and `ended: 'bound'`. That is wrong whenever the call is billed late. Before this PR, no calls gave `null`. The image door's own comment says a cut-short run must be unknown, never 0. The audio door should return `null` when `ended !== 'done'` and no summary exists.

findings.summary: `response.clone().text()` is called outside the handler try/catch. If the clone throws, `serve()` rejects with the sink still open.
findings.failureScenario: If `clone()` throws (for example, a handler returned a Response whose body is already used or locked), `serve()` rejects. It rejects after `sink.answer` was never set and before `finish()` is called. The caller gets an unhandled 500 with no `agw-run-id`. The sink then lives until the 1-hour `RECORD_MAX_MS` bound, and its run is recorded late as `bound`. The 500 catch path just above handles this properly; the clone call should be guarded the same way.

findings.summary: The `lost` counter is only incremented in the wrapped `fetch` rejection path. A call whose usage event arrives after `sink.close()` is dropped with a warning and not counted. The cost can still be reported as complete.
findings.failureScenario: A late `call` event lands after `sink.close()` (a pcm stream that records just after the grace period). `record()` logs a warning and drops it, and `lost` does not move. The step reports `costUsd` as the sum of the earlier calls, or 0, even though one billed call was missed. This contradicts the new comment that says an unseen billed call makes the cost unknown.

findings.summary: A stream that fails after its 200 (summary status 500) makes the run fail with `door answered 500` and no cause. The error text is only read from the clone when the answered status is >= 400.
findings.failureScenario: A pcm speech stream is answered 200 and then dies upstream. `sink.answered.status` is 200 and `answered.errorText` resolves to `''`, which `errorTextOf` turns into null. The run error becomes `door answered 500` with no cause, and the operator cannot tell it was a mid-stream failure. The message also says 'answered 500', although the caller was answered 200. A distinct message such as 'stream failed after 200' would be accurate.

findings.summary: `errorKindOfStatus` treats only 400/413/422 as the caller's fault. Other client-fault statuses (401, 403, 404, 405, 415, 429) become kind `error`, indistinguishable from real server failures.
findings.failureScenario: A studio or Hermes client posts to an unknown model (404), the wrong media type (415) or the wrong method, or hits a rate limit (429). The door run now ends `failed` with kind `error`. Failure-rate dashboards, alerts and evals count these as platform errors. A generic 4xx rule (`status >= 400 && status < 500 && status !== 408/429`) would be more consistent. The audio and image doors share this helper, so both inherit the gap.

findings.summary: The run now throws a `WorkflowError` after the step is journaled. The run always ends `failed` for any answered status >= 400 unless the end was `client-gone`. On a retry or resume, the throw replays on every run from the journaled output.
findings.failureScenario: A request that the client aborted just after the handler returned an upstream error ends as `client-gone` and stays `done`. If the client abort and `finish()` race the other way, the same request ends `failed`. The outcome of the run depends on timing, because `sink.ended` is set by whichever of `finish` or the cancel callback runs first. The test only covers the deterministic cases.

findings.summary: One test asserts the 400 failure twice: the existing `badRun` block, then the newly added `bad400` block. Both call `failedRun` on the same run, so the second repeats the first.
findings.failureScenario: No runtime failure. The copy-paste duplication adds dead assertions (`failedRun(badRun)` after `failedRun(badRun as string)`) and makes the test harder to maintain. The second block should be deleted.
